paragraphs: Very dear and well beloved:

Considering how advantageous it would be to this realm to reestablish its foreign and domestic commerce, … we have resolved to create a council particularly devoted to commerce, to be held every fortnight in our presence, in which all the interests of merchants and the means conducive to the revival of commerce shall be considered and determined upon, as well as all that which concerns manufactures.

We also inform you that we are setting apart, among the expenses of our State, a million livres each year for the encouragement of manufactures and the increase of navigation, to say nothing of the considerable sums which we cause to be raised to supply the companies of the East and West Indies;
That we are working constantly to abolish all the tolls which are collected on the navigable rivers; …
That we will assist by money from our royal treasury all those who wish to reestablish old manufactures or to undertake new ones; …

… in order that, being informed of the favorable treatment which we desire to give them [the merchants of Marseilles], they may be the more desirous of applying themselves to commerce. Let them understand that for everything that concerns the welfare and advantage of the same they are to address themselves to Sieur Colbert. …

paragraphs: Having already made my protestations, not only against the illegality of this pretended Court, but also, that no earthly power can justly call me (who am your King) in question as a delinquent, … the duty I owe to God in the preservation of the true liberty of my people will not suffer me at this time to be silent … .

There is no proceeding just against any man, but what is warranted, either by God's laws or the municipal laws of the country where he lives. Now I am most confident this day's proceeding cannot be warranted by God's laws; for, on the contrary, the authority of obedience unto Kings is clearly warranted, and strictly commanded in both the Old and New Testament … . Then for the law of this land, I am no less confident, that no learned lawyer will affirm that an impeachment can lie against the King, they all going in his name: and one of their maxims is, that the King can do no wrong. … But how the House of Commons can erect a Court of Judicature, which was never one itself (as is well known to all lawyers) I leave to God and the world to judge. …

paragraphs: The making Peace and War is the undoubted Prerogative of the Crown; yet such is the just Confidence I place in you, that at the Opening of this Session I acquainted you, That a Negotiation for a General Peace was begun; and afterwards, by Messages, I promised to communicate to you the Terms of Peace, before the same should be concluded. …

The Assuring of the Protestant Succession, as by Law established, in the House of Hanover, to these Kingdoms, being what I have nearest at Heart, particular Care is taken, not only to have that acknowledged in the strongest Terms, but to have an additional Security, by the Removal of that Person out of the Dominions of France, who has pretended to disturb this Settlement.*

The Apprehension that Spain and the West Indies might be united to France was the chief Inducement to begin this War; and the effectual Preventing of such an Union was the Principle I laid down at the Commencement of this Treaty. …

I can, therefore, now tell you, That France at last is brought to offer, that the Duke of Anjou** shall, for himself and his Descendants, renounce forever all Claim to the Crown of France. … France and Spain are now more effectually divided than ever. And thus, by the Blessing of God, will a real Balance of Power be fixed in Europe, and remain liable to as few Accidents as Human Affairs can be exempted from. …

Our Interest is so deeply concerned in the Trade of North America, that I have used my utmost Endeavours to adjust that Article in the most beneficial Manner. France consents to restore to us the whole Bay and Streights of Hudson; to deliver up the Island of Newfoundland, with Placentia, and to make an absolute Cession of Annapolis, with the rest of Nova Scotia or Acadia. …

Our Mediterranean Trade, and the British Interest and Influence in those Parts, will be secured by the Possession of Gibraltar and Port Mahon, with the whole Island of Minorca, which are offered to remain in my Hands. …

But the Part which we have born in the Prosecution of this War, intitling us to some Distinction in the Terms of Peace, I have insisted and obtained, That the Asiento, or Contract for furnishing the Spanish West-Indies with Negroes,*** shall be made with us for the Term of Thirty Years, in the same Manner as it has been enjoyed by the French for these Ten Years past.

paragraphs: The States bordering upon Poland have so often been involved in the disorders which have arisen during interregnums in that kingdom, that the experience of the past would in any case have led the neighboring powers to occupy themselves seriously with the affairs of that State the moment that the throne became vacant by the death of King Augustus III. …

… Everything seemed to promise a firm peace for both Poland and her neighbors, but unhappily the spirit of discord took possession of a portion of the nation, and destroyed in an instant all these hopes. Citizens armed themselves against one another, factions usurped the legitimate authority, which they abused in utter contempt of law, good order, and public security. Justice, the police, commerce, yes, agriculture itself, all were destroyed. …

… These powers have agreed accordingly to attempt to reach without loss of time a common understanding, in order to restore peace and good order in Poland, and establish the ancient constitution of this State and the liberties of the nation upon a sound basis. …

… They all had considerable claims upon various possessions of the republic. … Consequently his Majesty the King of Prussia, her Majesty the Empress, Queen of Hungary and Bohemia, and her Imperial Majesty of all the Russias, having mutually set forth their rights and claims, and having come to an agreement, will each take an equivalent of the district to which they lay claim, and will put themselves in effective possession of those portions of Poland which are calculated to serve hereafter as the most natural and secure boundary between them. …

paragraphs: The great Reformer's predecessors were fully conscious of this condition of things, and did what they could to remedy it. … Their programme included the reorganisation of the armed forces, and, as an inevitable consequence, the improvement of the finances,—the development of the economic resources of the country,—and the encouragement of foreign commerce. They admitted the necessity of more direct intercourse and co-operation with foreign countries. …

Then we come to Peter. What other, what new thing did he do? Nothing, or, at most, very little indeed. The programme above referred to was his programme; he enlarged it a little, added the Reform of the national customs; he modified the nature of the intercourse already in existence with the Western world; but he, too, left the foundations of the political edifice he had inherited, intact … . It was begun before his time,—what he did was to change the conditions under which it was to be carried on in future. The new factor was, in the first place, the endless war, which, for twenty long years, was to inspire, direct and drive him forward … . In the second place, we have the tastes, habits of mind, manias and fancies, which the gifted but whimsical ruler owed to his education, … and his intercourse with Europe. … Finally, the Reformer's personal temperament, which endued all his measures with qualities of violence, excess and hastiness, both painful and disconcerting to every one they affected, must be taken into account. What had been a peaceful evolution became, in consequence of these peculiarities, a revolution. …
… Peter, in a few years, had performed the work of several centuries. It may be doubted whether this sudden bound across time and space was an unmixed benefit. …
… The war made military reforms a first necessity, and these called forth financial measures, which, in their turn, made economic enterprises indispensable.

paragraphs: When the Parisians lost sight of their Broussel* they were like madmen, shouting through the streets that they were lost, that they would have their protector restored to them, that they would die, every one of them, cheerfully in his behalf. They assembled, they stretched chains across the streets, and in a few hours they erected barricades in every quarter of the town. …

The Coadjutor of Paris [Jean-François-Paul de Gondi, afterwards Cardinal de Retz], who, from inordinate ambition, had inclinations that were far from wishing to endeavour to remedy these evils, was also sent. … he went out on foot with his hood and rochet; and mingling with the crowd he reproved the people, shouted peace to them, and pointed out the obedience they owed to the king … .

The populace replied to what he said to them with respect for his person, but with audacity and anger against the idea of what they owed to the king. They demanded their protector, with protestations that they would never be pacified until he was returned to them; and without considering the respect they owed to the Grand-Master, the Maréchal de La Meilleraye, they flung stones at him, overwhelmed him with insults, and, in threatening him, uttered horrible imprecations against the queen and her minister. Against the latter they launched such insolence as deserved the gibbet if the king had been master … .
… Kings flatter themselves readily; our regent did so, and being born with intrepid courage, she ridiculed the emotions of the populace and could not believe they would ever do her any serious harm.

paragraphs: The state of monarchy is the supremest thing upon earth; for kings are not only God's lieutenants upon earth, and sit upon God's throne, but even by God himself they are called gods. …

Kings are justly called gods, for that they exercise a manner or resemblance of divine power upon earth; for if you will consider the attributes to God, you shall see how they agree in the person of a king. God hath power to create or destroy, make or unmake at his pleasure, to give life or send death, to judge all and to be judged nor accountable to none, to raise low things and to make high things low at his pleasure, and to God are both soul and body due. And the like power have kings: they make and unmake their subjects, they have power of raising and casting down, of life and of death, judges over all their subjects and in all causes and yet accountable to none but God only. …
I would wish you to be careful to avoid three things in the matter of grievances:
First, that you do not meddle with the main points of government; that is my craft … to meddle with that were to lessen me. … I must not be taught my office.

Secondly, I would not have you meddle with such ancient rights of mine as I have received from my predecessors … . All novelties are dangerous as well in a politic as in a natural body, and therefore I would be loath to be quarreled in my ancient rights and possessions; for that were to judge me unworthy of that which my predecessors had and left me. …

paragraphs: Having by our late labours and hazards made it appear to the world at how high a rate we value our just freedom, and God having so far owned our cause as to deliver the enemies thereof into our hands, we do now hold ourselves bound in mutual duty to each other to take the best care we can for the future to avoid both the danger of returning into a slavish condition and the chargeable remedy of another war … . In order whereunto we declare:—

[I.] That the people of England, being at this day very unequally distributed by Counties, Cities, and Boroughs for the election of their deputies in Parliament, ought to be more indifferently proportioned according to the number of the inhabitants … .
III. That the people do, of course, choose themselves a Parliament once in two years … .

IV. That the power of this, and all future Representatives of this Nation, is inferior only to theirs who choose them, and doth extend, without the consent or concurrence of any other person or persons, to the enacting, altering, and repealing of laws, to the erecting and abolishing of offices and courts, to the appointing, removing, and calling to account magistrates and officers of all degrees, to the making war and peace, to the treating with foreign States, and, generally, to whatsoever is not expressly or impliedly reserved by the represented to themselves: Which are as followeth.
1. That matters of religion and the ways of God's worship are not at all entrusted by us to any human power … .

4. That in all laws made or to be made every person may be bound alike, and that no tenure, estate, charter, degree, birth, or place do confer any exemption from the ordinary course of legal proceedings whereunto others are subjected. …
These things we declare to be our native rights, and therefore are agreed and resolved to maintain them with our utmost possibilities against all opposition whatsoever … .

paragraphs: Whereas the late king James the Second by the assistance of divers evil counsellors, judges and ministers employed by him did endeavour to subvert and extirpate the Protestant religion and the laws and liberties of this kingdom.
By assuming and exercising a power of dispensing with and suspending of laws, and the execution of laws, without consent of parliament. …
By levying money for and to the use of the crown, by pretence of prerogative, for other time and in other manner than the same was granted by parliament.
By raising and keeping a standing army within this kingdom in time of peace, without consent of parliament, and quartering of soldiers contrary to law. …
… do in the first place (as their ancestors in like case have usually done) for the vindicating and asserting their ancient rights and liberties, declare:
That the pretended power of suspending of laws or the execution of laws by regal authority without consent of parliament is illegal. …
That the levying money for or to the use of the crown by pretence of prerogative without grant of parliament for a longer time or in other manner than the same is or shall be granted is illegal. …
That the raising or keeping a standing army within the kingdom in time of peace unless it be with consent of parliament is against law. …
That election of members of parliament ought to be free.
That the freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in parliament ought not to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of parliament. …
And that for redress of all grievances and for the amending, strengthening and preserving of the laws parliaments ought to be held frequently.

paragraphs: This is the war* to which we owe the National Debt, the Bank of England, the growth of the moneyed interest. …

Two of our greatest writers, to speak truly, our two greatest writers, Burke and Macaulay, have taken pains to show that the Revolution of 1688 was not revolutionary but conservative, that it was little more than a rectification of recent error, and a return to ancient principles. … No change took place in the governing class. The gentry who managed the affairs of the county managed the affairs of the country after 1688 as they had done before. There was no transfer of force from the aristocratic element of society to the democratic. …

And yet it is the greatest thing done by the English nation. It established the State upon a contract, and set up the doctrine that a breach of contract forfeited the crown … . Parliament gave the crown, and gave it under conditions. Parliament became supreme in administration as well as in legislation. The king became its servant on good behaviour, liable to dismissal for himself or his ministers. All this was not restitution, but inversion. Passive obedience had been the law of England. Conditional obedience and the right of resistance became the law. Authority was limited and regulated and controlled. … The great achievement is that this was done without bloodshed, without vengeance, without exclusion of entire parties … . The Act itself was narrow, spiritless, confused, tame, and unsatisfactory. It was perfectly compatible with the oppression of class by class, and of the country by the State, as the agent of a class.

paragraphs: This business is the clothing trade, for the convenience of which the houses are thus scattered and spread upon the sides of the hills, as above, even from the bottom to the top; the reason is this; such has been the bounty of nature to this otherwise frightful country, that two things essential to the business, as well as to the ease of the people are found here, … I mean coals and running water upon the tops of the highest hills … .
… we could see that almost at every house there was a tenter, and almost on every tenter a piece of cloth, or kersie, or shalloon, for they are the three articles of that country's labour … .

Then, as every clothier must keep a horse, perhaps two, to fetch and carry for the use of his manufacture, (viz.) to fetch home his wooll and his provisions from the market, to carry his yarn to the spinners, his manufacture to the fulling mill, and, when finished, to the market to be sold, and the like … .

… Among the manufacturers houses are likewise scattered an infinite number of cottages or small dwellings, in which dwell the workmen which are employed, the women and children of whom, are always busy carding, spinning, &c. so that no hands being unemploy'd, all can gain their bread, even from the youngest to the antient; hardly any thing above four years old, but its hands are sufficient to it self.

This is the reason also why we saw so few people without doors; but if we knock'd at the door of any of the master manufacturers, we presently saw a house full of lusty fellows, some at the dye-fat, some dressing the cloths, some in the loom, some one thing, some another, all hard at work, and full employed upon the manufacture, and all seeming to have sufficient business.

paragraphs: … The whole internal history of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, not only in Germany but everywhere else, is summed up in the opposition of the economic policy of the state to that of the town, the district, and the several Estates; the whole foreign history is summed up in the opposition to one another of the separate interests of the newly rising states, each of which sought to obtain and retain its place in the circle of European nations, and in that foreign trade which now included America and India. …

Only he who thus conceives of mercantilism will understand it; in its innermost kernel it is nothing but state making—not state making in a narrow sense, but state making and national-economy making at the same time … . The essence of the system lies not in some doctrine of money, or of the balance of trade; not in tariff barriers, protective duties, or navigation laws; but in something far greater:—namely, in the total transformation of society and its organisation, as well as of the state and its institutions, in the replacing of a local and territorial economic policy by that of the national state. …

The struggle against the great nobility, the towns, the corporations, and provinces, the economic as well as political blending of these isolated groups into a larger whole, the struggle for uniform measures and coinage, for a well-ordered system of currency and credit, for uniform laws and uniform administration, for freer and more active traffic within the land,—this it was which created a new division of labour, a new prosperity, and which liberated a thousand forces towards progress.
P9.attribution: Gustav Schmoller, German economist and historian, The Mercantile System and Its Historical Significance, first published in German in 1884
P9.translation: Translated by W. J. Ashley (New York and London: Macmillan, 1896), pp. 50–51; adapted

paragraphs: For the increase of the shipping and the encouragement of the navigation of this nation, which under the good providence and protection of God is so great a means of the welfare and safety of this Commonwealth: be it enacted … that from and after the first day of December, one thousand six hundred fifty and one, and from thence forwards, no goods or commodities whatsoever of the growth, production or manufacture of Asia, Africa or America, or of any part thereof … as well of the English plantations as others, shall be imported or brought into this Commonwealth of England, or into Ireland, or any other lands, islands, plantations, or territories to this Commonwealth belonging, or in their possession, in any other ship or ships, vessel or vessels whatsoever, but only in such as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of this Commonwealth, or the plantations thereof, as the proprietors or right owners thereof; and whereof the master and mariners are also for the most part of them of the people of this Commonwealth, under the penalty of the forfeiture and loss of all the goods that shall be imported contrary to this act … .

And it is further enacted … that no goods or commodities of the growth, production, or manufacture of Europe, or of any part thereof, shall … be imported or brought into this Commonwealth of England … in any ship or ships, vessel or vessels whatsoever, but in such as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of this Commonwealth, as the true owners and proprietors thereof, and in no other, except only such foreign ships and vessels as do truly and properly belong to the people of that country or place, of which the said goods are the growth, production or manufacture … .

And it is further enacted … that no sort of cod-fish, ling, herring, pilchard, or any other kind of salted fish, usually fished for and caught by the people of this nation … shall from henceforth be imported into this Commonwealth … but only such as shall be caught in vessels that do or shall truly and properly belong to the people of this nation … .

paragraphs: In some of your letters which I do not recollect, you speak (with honest indignation) of the treachery and chicanery of the natives.*—My good friend, you should remember from whom they learnt those vices:—the first Christian visitors found them a simple, harmless people—but the cursed avidity for wealth urged these first visitors (and all the succeeding ones) to such acts of deception—and even wanton cruelty—that the poor ignorant natives soon learnt to turn the knavish and diabolical arts which they soon imbibed—upon their teachers.

I am sorry to observe that the practice of your country (which as a resident I love—and for its freedom, and for the many blessings I enjoy in it, shall ever have my warmest wishes—prayers—and blessings;) I say, it is with reluctance that I must observe your country's conduct has been uniformly wicked in the East—West Indies—and even on the coast of Guinea.—The grand object of English navigators—indeed of all Christian navigators—is money—money—money—for which I do not pretend to blame them.—Commerce was meant, by the goodness of the Deity, to diffuse the various goods of the earth into every part—to unite mankind in the blessed chains of brotherly love—society—and mutual dependence … .—In Africa, the poor wretched natives—blessed with the most fertile and luxuriant soil—are rendered so much the more miserable for what Providence meant as a blessing:—the Christians' abominable traffic for slaves—and the horrid cruelty and treachery of the petty Kings—encouraged by their Christian customers—who carry them strong liquors, to enflame their national madness—and powder and bad fire arms, to furnish them with the hellish means of killing and kidnapping.—But enough—it is a subject that sours my blood … .
P11.attribution: Ignatius Sancho, writer of African descent who had been enslaved as a child and later ran a grocery shop in London, letter to a young English friend working in India, 1778, published in 1782
P11.translation: Text from Letters of the Late Ignatius Sancho, an African, 3rd ed. (London, 1784), letter 68 (Project Gutenberg transcription); adapted

paragraphs: Praised be our Lord God forever for granting our nation such a victory and such glory as was never heard of in all times past! The whole camp of the enemy, with their artillery and untold treasure, has fallen into our hands. They are now retreating in great confusion, and the approaches to the town, the camp, and the open fields are covered with their corpses. …
… The grand vizier lost all his rich treasure and barely escaped, on horseback, with nothing but the coat on his back, and I have become his heir and successor. …
… It cannot be denied that they defended themselves bravely, especially the companies of janizaries who guarded the approaches to the camp and so bore the brunt of the battle. …

This morning early I went into the town and found that it could not have held out five days longer. Never have the eyes of men beheld so great damage done in so brief a time; great masses of stone and rock have been broken up and tossed about in heaps by the enemy's mines, and the imperial castle is riddled with holes and ruined by their cannon balls.

… Then (when the victory was won) I was surrounded by the elector of Bavaria, Prince von Waldeck, and many more of the imperial princes, who embraced and kissed me; … Finally, the governor of Vienna, Count von Stahrenberg, accompanied by a great crowd of people of both high and low degree, came out to greet me, all kissing and petting me and calling me their savior. …
… Let Christendom rejoice and thank the Lord our God … .

paragraphs: The sensible grief which we feel for the loss of a prince, whom his excellent qualities and the strict ties of blood rendered most dear to us, is infinitely increased by the proofs which he gave us at his death, of his justice and love for his faithful subjects, and the desire he showed to maintain, after his death, the general quiet of all Europe, and the happiness of his kingdoms. We will on our part contribute to the one and the other … . All our care henceforth will be to raise, by an inviolable and most strict correspondence, the Spanish Monarchy to the highest pitch of grandeur it has ever arrived at. We accept, in favor of our Grandson, the Duke of Anjou, the Will of the deceased Catholic king … .

… We shall exhort him to remember his birth, to preserve the love of his country, but, above all, to maintain forever that peace and perfect good understanding so necessary to the common happiness of our subjects and his own, which has always been the principal object of our wishes … .

paragraphs: Whereas Charles II King of Spain, of most glorious memory, being not long since dead without issue, his sacred Imperial Majesty has claimed the succession in the kingdoms and provinces of the deceased king as lawfully belonging to his august family, but the Most Christian King, aiming at the same succession for his grandson, the Duke of Anjou, and pretending that a right did accrue to him by a certain Will of the deceased king, has usurped the possession of the entire inheritance or Spanish monarchy for the aforesaid Duke of Anjou and invaded by his arms the provinces of the Spanish Low Countries and the duchy of Milan, … and by this and many other ways the kingdoms of France and Spain are so closely united and cemented that they may seem henceforward not to be otherwise considered than as one and the same kingdom.

paragraphs: … God having at last permitted that our people should enjoy perfect peace, we, no longer absorbed in protecting them from our enemies, are able to profit by this truce (which we have ourselves facilitated), and devote our whole attention to the means of accomplishing the designs of our said grandfather and father, which we have consistently kept before us since our succession to the crown.

And now we perceive, with thankful acknowledgment of God's aid, that our endeavors have attained their proposed end, inasmuch as the better and the greater part of our subjects of the said R.P.R.* have embraced the Catholic faith. And since by this fact the execution of the Edict of Nantes and of all that has ever been ordained in favor of the said R.P.R. has been rendered nugatory, we have determined that we can do nothing better, in order wholly to obliterate the memory of the troubles, the confusion, and the evils which the progress of this false religion has caused in this kingdom, … than entirely to revoke the said Edict of Nantes … .
… II. We forbid our subjects of the R.P.R. to meet any more for the exercise of the said religion in any place or private house, under any pretext whatever, … .

… IV. We enjoin all ministers of the said R.P.R., who do not choose to become converts and to embrace the Catholic, apostolic, and Roman religion, to leave our kingdom and the territories subject to us within a fortnight of the publication of our present edict … .

… X. We repeat our most express prohibition to all our subjects of the said R.P.R., together with their wives and children, against leaving our kingdom, lands, and territories subject to us, or transporting their goods and effects therefrom under penalty, as respects the men, of being sent to the galleys, and as respects the women, of imprisonment and confiscation.

paragraphs: I mentioned in the relation of the former year the tsar's coming out of his own country; on which I will now enlarge. He came this winter [early 1698] over to England and stayed some months among us. I waited often on him, and was ordered both by the king and the archbishop and bishops to attend upon him and to offer him such informations of our religion and constitution as he was willing to receive. I had good interpreters, so I had much free discourse with him. He is a man of a very hot temper, soon inflamed and very brutal in his passion. … He wants not capacity, and has a larger measure of knowledge than might be expected from his education, which was very indifferent. …

He is mechanically turned, and seems designed by nature rather to be a ship carpenter than a great prince. This was his chief study and exercise while he stayed here. He wrought much with his own hands and made all about him work at the models of ships. He told me he designed a great fleet at Azuph [i.e. Azov] and with it to attack the Turkish empire. …

He was desirous to understand our doctrine, but he did not seem disposed to mend matters in Moscovy. He was, indeed, resolved to encourage learning and to polish his people by sending some of them to travel in other countries and to draw strangers to come and live among them. …

After I had seen him often, and had conversed much with him, I could not but adore the depth of the providence of God that had raised up such a furious man to so absolute an authority over so great a part of the world. …

practice.stem: The events Motteville describes are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Protestant revolts in France after Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes
options.B: Peasant uprisings against feudal dues on the eve of the French Revolution
options.C: Resistance to new taxes and to royal power while Louis XIV was a child
options.D: Riots in Paris over the cost of France's war with the Dutch Republic

practice.explanation: In 1648 Louis XIV was nine years old. His mother ruled for him with Cardinal Mazarin, and they wanted new taxes to pay for war. Judges of the Parlement of Paris fought the taxes. When the queen had Broussel arrested, Paris rose up. This began the revolts called the Fronde (1648–1653).

whyNot.A: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, almost forty years after these riots of 1648.
whyNot.B: The French Revolution began in 1789, more than a century later. This crowd is in Paris and is defending a judge, not attacking feudal dues.
whyNot.D: France's war with the Dutch Republic began in 1672. In 1648 the crowd wanted the queen to free Broussel.

practice.hint: Who was ruling France in 1648, and why might a judge of the Parlement have angered the queen and her minister?

practice.stem: Motteville's account of the riot was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.A: Her loyalty to the queen, whom she served at court
options.B: Her support for Broussel and the judges of the Parlement
options.C: Her role as one of the leaders of the revolt in Paris
options.D: Her experience as a Protestant living under a Catholic king

practice.explanation: Motteville served Queen Anne and lived at court. She calls the crowd "madmen" and praises the queen's "intrepid courage." She saw the Fronde from the queen's side, and a historian should keep that in mind.

whyNot.B: Motteville says the crowd acted "like madmen" and that their insults "deserved the gibbet." She does not take Broussel's side.
whyNot.C: Motteville was with the queen at the palace, not in the streets. She was frightened by the riot, not leading it.
whyNot.D: Motteville was a Catholic attendant of a Catholic queen. Nothing in her account suggests she was a Protestant.

practice.hint: Look at the attribution. Where did Motteville live and work, and how does she describe the crowd?

practice.stem: In the long term, revolts like the one Motteville describes most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: Louis XIV's decision to abolish the Parlement of Paris and replace its judges
options.B: Louis XIV's efforts to keep great nobles under watch at Versailles
options.C: Louis XIV's creation of an elected assembly to approve new taxes
options.D: Louis XIV's grant of self-government to the city of Paris

practice.explanation: As a boy, Louis XIV saw nobles and the people of Paris rise against the crown. As king, he ruled without a chief minister and used royal officials called intendants. He also brought great nobles to live at his court at Versailles, where he could watch them.

whyNot.A: Louis XIV limited the Parlement's right to protest his laws, but he did not abolish it. The Parlement of Paris still existed in 1789.
whyNot.C: Louis XIV never called the Estates-General, France's assembly of the three estates. It did not meet between 1614 and 1789.
whyNot.D: Louis XIV distrusted Paris and moved his court to Versailles. He did not give the city self-government.

practice.hint: How might a king who lived through these riots as a child treat powerful nobles and the city of Paris later on?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes James I's main argument in the speech?

options.A: Kings must follow the ancient laws that Parliament has passed.
options.B: Parliament should advise the king on the main points of government.
options.C: Kings get their power from God and answer to God alone.
options.D: Subjects may resist a king who governs against the laws of God.

practice.explanation: James says kings are "God's lieutenants upon earth." He says they answer to God alone. This is the idea of the divine right of kings.

whyNot.A: James warns Parliament not to question his "ancient rights" and says kings are "accountable to none but God only."
whyNot.B: James tells Parliament "that you do not meddle with the main points of government; that is my craft."
whyNot.D: James says kings answer to God, not to their subjects. He gives subjects no right to resist.

practice.hint: To whom does James say a king must answer?

practice.stem: Claims like those in James I's speech most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: The Wars of the Roses between rival noble families for the English throne
options.B: Henry VIII's break with the pope and creation of the Church of England
options.C: The union of the English and Scottish parliaments into one Parliament in 1707
options.D: Conflict between the Stuart kings and Parliament that led to civil war

practice.explanation: James I and his son Charles I claimed powers that many in Parliament rejected. They argued most about taxes and religion. Charles I ruled without Parliament from 1629 to 1640, and in 1642 war broke out between king and Parliament.

whyNot.A: The Wars of the Roses ended in the 1480s, more than a century before James became king of England in 1603.
whyNot.B: Henry VIII broke with the pope in the 1530s, long before this speech.
whyNot.C: England and Scotland joined their parliaments in 1707 for political and economic reasons, long after the Stuarts' quarrels over divine right.

practice.hint: Put the choices in time order. Which one came after 1610 and grew out of arguments about royal power?

practice.stem: James I's view of monarchy is most similar to the views of which of the following writers?

options.A: John Locke
options.B: Baron de Montesquieu
options.C: John Lilburne
options.D: Bishop Bossuet

practice.explanation: Bossuet was a French bishop. He wrote that kings rule as God's agents and answer only to God. Like James I, he defended the divine right of kings.

whyNot.A: Locke argued that government rests on the consent of the people and that people may resist a ruler who abuses power.
whyNot.B: Montesquieu argued for separating the powers of government so that no single ruler holds them all.
whyNot.C: Lilburne was a leader of the Levellers, who wanted the people's elected representatives to hold supreme power.

practice.hint: Which writer defended absolute monarchy in France?

practice.stem: The Agreement of the People is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Debate over how to govern England after Charles II returned to the throne
options.B: Debate over how to govern England after Parliament's army defeated Charles I
options.C: Protests against James II's efforts to give Catholics high offices
options.D: Quarrels between James I and Parliament over the divine right of kings

practice.explanation: By 1646 Parliament's New Model Army had beaten Charles I. Soldiers and their allies, the Levellers, then argued about the next government. The Agreement asked for fairer seats in Parliament, elections every two years, and rights that no government could take away.

whyNot.A: Charles II returned to the throne in 1660, more than twelve years after this plan was written.
whyNot.C: James II ruled from 1685 to 1688, long after 1647.
whyNot.D: James I died in 1625. By 1647 his son, Charles I, had lost a civil war.

practice.hint: The writers say God has delivered "the enemies" of their cause "into our hands." Whom had they just defeated?

practice.stem: Members of which group would most likely have opposed the Agreement of the People?

options.A: Royalists who supported Charles I
options.B: Leveller writers in London
options.C: Radical soldiers in the New Model Army
options.D: Baptist congregations seeking freedom of worship

practice.explanation: Article IV gives Parliament its power "without the consent or concurrence of any other person." That leaves out the king and the House of Lords. Royalists believed the king must help make the laws, so they would have opposed the plan.

whyNot.B: The Levellers helped write the Agreement and spread its ideas in pamphlets.
whyNot.C: Radical soldiers chose agents, called agitators, to speak for their regiments, and plans like this one were presented to the army's council.
whyNot.D: Article 1 says religion is not "entrusted by us to any human power," which matches what Baptists and other sects wanted.

practice.hint: Article IV says who would make the laws. Who is left out?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the plan in the Agreement and the settlement after the Glorious Revolution of 1688–1689?

options.A: The 1689 settlement gave the vote to men without property, while the Agreement limited voting to landowners.
options.B: The 1689 settlement made Catholicism the state religion, while the Agreement banned any official state church.
options.C: The 1689 settlement kept a king and House of Lords, while the Agreement made an elected body supreme.
options.D: The 1689 settlement ended Parliament's control over taxes, while the Agreement kept that control.

practice.explanation: After 1689 England still had a monarch and a House of Lords. Only some men could vote for the House of Commons, and the voting rules differed from place to place. The Agreement would have made the elected Parliament supreme, with power "inferior only to theirs who choose them."

whyNot.A: The 1689 settlement did not change who could vote. The Agreement asks for seats based on "the number of the inhabitants" and does not limit voting to landowners.
whyNot.B: The 1689 settlement barred Catholics from the throne and kept the Church of England as the state church.
whyNot.D: The Bill of Rights made it illegal for the crown to raise money without Parliament's consent, so Parliament kept control of taxes.

practice.hint: Article IV says who holds supreme power under the Agreement. Who still shared power in England after 1689?

practice.stem: The image is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Glorious Revolution and the passage of the Bill of Rights
options.B: The Spanish Armada's attempt to invade England and restore Catholicism
options.C: The breakdown of royal authority during the English Civil War
options.D: Louis XIV's wars against the Dutch Republic

practice.explanation: Hobbes wrote Leviathan in Paris in the last years of the English Civil Wars (1642–1651). In those years king and Parliament fought, and Charles I was executed. Hobbes argued that only one supreme power, held by a single ruler or by an assembly, could stop such chaos.

whyNot.A: The Glorious Revolution took place in 1688–1689, almost forty years after the book was published.
whyNot.B: The Spanish Armada sailed in 1588, more than sixty years before 1651.
whyNot.D: Louis XIV's war against the Dutch began in 1672, two decades after the book appeared.

practice.hint: The book came out in London in 1651. What had England just lived through?

practice.stem: The artist most likely made the giant's body out of many small people in order to suggest that

options.A: the ruler's power comes from the people, joined together under one sovereign
options.B: the people have the right to overthrow a ruler who breaks the law
options.C: the ruler shares power equally with an assembly elected by the people
options.D: the people should obey the Church rather than the king

practice.explanation: The tiny people make up the giant's body. This shows the people joining together to create one ruler. Hobbes said people give their power to that ruler, who must then be obeyed to keep the peace.

whyNot.B: The people form part of the ruler's body; they are not shown as a force that can remove him. Hobbes said people could defend their own lives, but he gave them no right to overthrow the sovereign. That idea is closer to John Locke's.
whyNot.C: No assembly appears in the image. One crowned figure holds all the power.
whyNot.D: The giant himself holds the crozier, a symbol of church power, so the ruler is over the Church.

practice.hint: What do the tiny people make up? Who holds the sword and the crozier?

practice.stem: Hobbes's idea of the sovereign, as shown in the image, differs most from James I's view of kingship in that Hobbes

options.A: gives the people the right to remove a ruler who breaks the law
options.B: argues that the Church should be independent of the ruler
options.C: says that a ruler must share the making of laws with an elected Parliament
options.D: bases the ruler's power on the people's agreement, not on God's choice

practice.explanation: James I said God chooses kings. Hobbes said the ruler's power starts when people agree to join together under one ruler. Both men said subjects must obey, but they explained the ruler's power in different ways.

whyNot.A: Hobbes wanted people to obey the sovereign so that the country would not fall back into civil war. He did not give them a right to remove a ruler.
whyNot.B: The giant holds the crozier, a symbol of church power. Hobbes put the Church under the sovereign.
whyNot.C: Hobbes wanted all power held by one sovereign. The image shows one crowned figure holding both the sword and the crozier.

practice.hint: Both men wanted subjects to obey. Where does each one say the ruler's power comes from?

practice.stem: The Bill of Rights is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Parliament's victory over Charles I and the creation of a republic
options.B: Parliament's removal of a Catholic king who had ruled without its consent
options.C: The return of the Stuart kings after the collapse of the Commonwealth
options.D: William III's war against Louis XIV over the throne of Spain

practice.explanation: James II was a Catholic king. He was accused of setting aside laws and keeping an army without Parliament's consent. In 1688 he fled, and Parliament gave the throne to William and Mary. In 1689 it listed rights that rulers could not take away.

whyNot.A: Charles I was defeated in the 1640s and executed in 1649. The Bill of Rights names "the late king James the Second."
whyNot.C: Charles II returned to the throne in 1660. The Bill of Rights was passed after his brother, James II, lost the throne in 1688.
whyNot.D: The War of the Spanish Succession began in 1701–1702, more than ten years after the Bill of Rights.

practice.hint: Which king does the Bill of Rights accuse, and what had he done?

practice.stem: The rights declared in the Bill of Rights most directly protected the power of which group?

options.A: Catholic subjects of the English crown
options.B: Gentry and nobles in Parliament
options.C: Urban workers who owned no property
options.D: Officers of the king's standing army

practice.explanation: Parliament had two houses. The House of Lords held nobles and bishops. The House of Commons was elected mostly by landowners. By limiting the king and protecting Parliament, the Bill of Rights protected these landowning gentry and nobles.

whyNot.A: The Bill of Rights accuses James II of trying "to subvert and extirpate the Protestant religion." It did not protect Catholics' power.
whyNot.C: Most men who voted for Parliament owned property, and the Bill of Rights did not widen the vote.
whyNot.D: The Bill of Rights says a standing army in peacetime needs the "consent of parliament." This limited the army instead of protecting its officers.

practice.hint: Many of the rights belong to "parliament." Who sat in Parliament in 1689?

practice.stem: The Bill of Rights best reflects which form of government?

options.A: Divine-right absolute monarchy
options.B: Republican commonwealth
options.C: Enlightened despotism
options.D: Constitutional monarchy

practice.explanation: In a constitutional monarchy, a king or queen rules within limits set by law. The Bill of Rights kept the monarchy. But the ruler now needed Parliament's consent for taxes and for a peacetime army.

whyNot.A: Divine-right thinkers said kings got their power from God and did not answer to their subjects. The Bill of Rights says the crown may not suspend laws or raise money without the "consent of parliament."
whyNot.B: England remained a monarchy: Parliament offered the crown to William and Mary.
whyNot.C: Enlightened despots, such as Frederick II of Prussia, made reforms by their own will in the later 1700s. The Bill of Rights limits the ruler by law.

practice.hint: Does England still have a king or queen after 1689? Is that ruler's power limited?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes Acton's main argument about the Revolution of 1688?

options.A: It moved power from the aristocracy to ordinary people through violence.
options.B: It kept the same ruling class but made Parliament supreme over the king.
options.C: It changed little, because the king kept full control of the government.
options.D: It succeeded mainly because it granted religious freedom to Catholics and dissenters.

practice.explanation: Acton says the same landowning class ruled after 1688. But he says the Revolution still changed English government. Parliament now gave the crown "under conditions," and "Conditional obedience" took the place of "Passive obedience."

whyNot.A: Acton says there was "no transfer of force from the aristocratic element of society to the democratic" and that it was done "without bloodshed."
whyNot.C: Acton says "Parliament became supreme" and the king became "its servant on good behaviour."
whyNot.D: Acton praises the Revolution for making Parliament supreme and the king's power conditional. He does not credit religious freedom for its success, and the Toleration Act of 1689 helped Protestant dissenters but not Catholics.

practice.hint: Acton begins with what did not change. Then he writes, "And yet." What does he say did change?

practice.stem: Which of the following, if true, would best support Acton's claim that "Parliament became supreme in administration as well as in legislation"?

options.A: After 1689, William III chose his ministers and kept them when Parliament objected.
options.B: After 1689, Parliament met just when the king decided to call it.
options.C: After 1689, the crown needed money voted by Parliament each year to pay its army.
options.D: After 1689, the gentry kept running local government in the counties.

practice.explanation: If the king needed Parliament's vote every year to pay his army, he could not rule without Parliament. After 1689 Parliament usually voted army money one year at a time. So it had to meet every year.

whyNot.A: A king who kept his ministers against Parliament's wishes would show royal power. This would weaken Acton's claim.
whyNot.B: If Parliament met just when the king chose, the king would still be in charge. This would weaken the claim.
whyNot.D: This fits Acton's point that the governing class did not change, but it says nothing about Parliament's power over the king.

practice.hint: Look for the choice that shows the king depending on Parliament.

practice.stem: Acton's statement that the war gave England "the National Debt, the Bank of England" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Dutch Republic lending money to Charles I during the English Civil War
options.B: The collapse of the South Sea Company's stock in the bubble of 1720
options.C: Britain's need to pay for the Seven Years' War against France
options.D: Government borrowing from investors to pay for long, costly wars

practice.explanation: England joined the war against Louis XIV's France in 1689 and fought until 1697. To pay for it, the government borrowed money from investors. In 1694 investors started the Bank of England to lend to the government. This long-term borrowing became the National Debt.

whyNot.A: The English Civil War ended decades before the Bank of England was founded in 1694.
whyNot.B: The South Sea Bubble burst in 1720, more than twenty-five years after the Bank of England was founded.
whyNot.C: The Seven Years' War (1756–1763) came long after the war Acton describes, which ended in 1697.

practice.hint: The footnote tells you which war Acton means. How did England pay for it?

practice.stem: The way of making cloth that Defoe describes is best identified as which of the following?

options.A: Factory production
options.B: Manorial farming
options.C: Guild workshops
options.D: Cottage industry

practice.explanation: Clothiers and a few hired men made cloth in their own houses. Women and children in nearby cottages carded and spun the wool. The clothier took the finished cloth to market. This home-based work is called cottage industry.

whyNot.A: Factories bring workers together under one roof to work machines. Defoe describes work done in many scattered houses and cottages.
whyNot.B: Under the manorial system, peasants farmed a lord's land and owed him labor. Defoe's clothiers make cloth "to be sold" at market.
whyNot.C: Guilds were town organizations that controlled who could practice a trade. Defoe describes families spread across the countryside, not town guild masters.

practice.hint: Where does the work take place, and who does it?

practice.stem: Which of the following changes in the European economy does the passage best illustrate?

options.A: Rural households making goods for distant markets, not just for their own use
options.B: Guilds tightening their control over cloth making in the countryside
options.C: Large steam-powered mills replacing work that had been done in homes
options.D: Landowners forcing peasants back into serfdom to keep them on the land

practice.explanation: Defoe shows country families making cloth to be sold at market. In the 1600s and 1700s, more and more rural households made goods for faraway buyers.

whyNot.B: Defoe describes clothiers and families working on their own, outside town guilds. Rural cloth making grew partly because it escaped guild rules.
whyNot.C: Steam-powered mills spread in the late 1700s and 1800s, after Defoe wrote in the 1720s. Here, cloth is made in houses.
whyNot.D: Serfdom grew stronger in eastern Europe, not in England. Defoe's workers are paid laborers and small clothiers.

practice.hint: Where does the finished cloth go after it is made?

practice.stem: Features of the region Defoe describes, such as coal and running water, would later most directly support which development?

options.A: The growth of commercial farming and enclosure
options.B: The growth of British trade with Asian markets
options.C: The growth of sugar plantations in the Caribbean
options.D: The growth of mechanized textile factories

practice.explanation: Running water could turn mill wheels, and coal could fuel steam engines. In the late 1700s and 1800s, cloth making in northern England moved into water-powered and then steam-powered factories. This was part of the Industrial Revolution.

whyNot.A: Commercial farming and enclosure changed how land was used. Coal and running water power machines, not farms.
whyNot.B: British trade with Asia grew through ships and trading companies such as the East India Company. It did not depend on coal and streams in Yorkshire.
whyNot.C: Caribbean sugar plantations depended on a warm climate and enslaved labor, not on coal and streams in Yorkshire.

practice.hint: What could running water and coal be used to power?

practice.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: Income per person fell in all three countries between 1688 and 1695.
options.B: England had a larger population than France in both years shown.
options.C: Taxes per person rose in all three countries between 1688 and 1695.
options.D: France collected less in total taxes than Holland in both years shown.

practice.explanation: Taxes per person rose in England (£0.36 to £1.20), in France (£0.75 to £1.25), and in Holland (£2.16 to £3.08). All three went up.

whyNot.A: Holland's income per person rose slightly, from £8.07 to £8.14.
whyNot.B: France had about 14 million people in 1688, more than twice England's 5.5 million.
whyNot.D: France collected £10.5 million in 1688 and £17.5 million in 1695, far more than Holland.

practice.hint: Compare the last column for each country in 1688 and in 1695.

practice.stem: The change in taxes between 1688 and 1695 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Thirty Years' War
options.B: The War of the Spanish Succession
options.C: The Nine Years' War
options.D: The English Civil War

practice.explanation: The Nine Years' War lasted from 1688 to 1697. France fought the Dutch Republic, England (from 1689), and their allies. Big armies and navies cost a lot of money. So all three countries raised taxes sharply.

whyNot.A: The Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, forty years before the first date in the table.
whyNot.B: The War of the Spanish Succession began in 1701, after the second date in the table.
whyNot.D: The English Civil War was fought in the 1640s, long before 1688.

practice.hint: Which war was being fought in 1695?

practice.stem: Which of the following best explains why Holland had the highest income per person in the table?

options.A: The Dutch Republic had more farmland per person than England or France.
options.B: The Dutch Republic received large amounts of silver from its mines in the Americas.
options.C: The Dutch Republic earned most of its income from large noble estates.
options.D: The Dutch Republic had grown rich from shipping, overseas trade, and banking.

practice.explanation: In the 1600s Dutch ships carried much of Europe's trade. The Dutch East India Company traded across Asia, and Amsterdam had Europe's leading bank. This trade made the Dutch the richest people per person in Europe.

whyNot.A: The Dutch Republic was small and crowded, with less land per person than England or France. Its wealth came mostly from trade.
whyNot.B: Spain, not the Dutch Republic, controlled the great silver mines of the Americas.
whyNot.C: Dutch wealth did not come mainly from noble estates. Merchants, shipping, and trade made the Dutch Republic rich.

practice.hint: What was the Dutch Republic best known for in the 1600s?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes Schmoller's main argument?

options.A: Mercantilism was mainly a way of building strong, unified states.
options.B: Mercantilism was mainly a belief that wealth means having gold and silver.
options.C: Mercantilism was mainly a plan to let merchants trade without government rules.
options.D: Mercantilism was mainly a way for towns and guilds to protect local markets.

practice.explanation: Schmoller says mercantilism was "nothing but state making." Rulers worked against the power of nobles, towns, guilds, and provinces. They wanted one economy with the same laws, coins, and measures for the whole state.

whyNot.B: Schmoller says the essence of the system "lies not in some doctrine of money."
whyNot.C: Schmoller describes states taking an active role in the economy, working for "uniform laws and uniform administration."
whyNot.D: Schmoller says mercantilism replaced "a local and territorial economic policy" with that of the national state. It worked against the towns and corporations.

practice.hint: Schmoller says what mercantilism is "in its innermost kernel." What does he say?

practice.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Schmoller's argument?

options.A: The Dutch provinces' success in keeping their own separate systems of taxes
options.B: Polish nobles' success in blocking royal efforts to raise taxes and armies
options.C: Colbert's efforts to remove tolls and set one tariff for much of France
options.D: Adam Smith's call for governments to stop regulating trade

practice.explanation: In the 1660s Colbert cut tolls and customs barriers inside France. His tariff of 1664 set one system of duties for a large part of the kingdom. This is the kind of national policy that Schmoller praises.

whyNot.A: Schmoller argues that states replaced local systems with national ones. Provinces keeping separate taxes would show the opposite.
whyNot.B: Schmoller says states struggled against "the great nobility." Nobles who blocked their king would show that struggle failing, not a national economy being built.
whyNot.D: Smith attacked mercantilism in 1776. His call for less regulation does not show states building national economies.

practice.hint: Schmoller praises "freer and more active traffic within the land." Which choice shows that happening?

practice.stem: Schmoller's positive view of mercantilism contrasts most strongly with the views of which of the following?

options.A: Jean-Baptiste Colbert
options.B: Adam Smith
options.C: Thomas Mun
options.D: Frederick William I of Prussia

practice.explanation: Adam Smith wrote The Wealth of Nations in 1776. He attacked the mercantile system. He said free trade and competition, not government control, make nations rich.

whyNot.A: Colbert, Louis XIV's minister, put mercantilist policies into practice in France.
whyNot.C: Mun was an English merchant whose book England's Treasure by Forraign Trade defended mercantilist ideas.
whyNot.D: Frederick William I built up Prussia's army and treasury with strict state control of the economy, much as Schmoller describes.

practice.hint: Which person argued that governments should leave trade more free?

practice.stem: The Navigation Act was mainly intended to

options.A: lower prices in England by opening its ports to ships from any nation
options.B: stop England's colonies from selling the goods they produced in England
options.C: end the trade in salted fish between England and the nations around it
options.D: build up English shipping at the expense of foreign carriers such as the Dutch

practice.explanation: The act says it is "for the increase of the shipping" of England. At the time, Dutch ships carried much of England's trade. The act tried to win that business for English ships and sailors.

whyNot.A: The act does the opposite: it limits foreign ships. Goods from Asia, Africa, and America must come in English or colonial ships. Goods from Europe may also come in ships of the country where they were made.
whyNot.B: The act lets goods from the colonies in, as long as they come in English or colonial ships.
whyNot.C: The act lets fish into England if it is caught in English vessels. It protects English fishermen; it does not end the trade.

practice.hint: Read the first line of the act. What does it say the act is for?

practice.stem: The Navigation Act is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Spain's control of trade between Europe and the East Indies
options.B: The Dutch lead in Europe's shipping and carrying trade
options.C: France's leading role in the Atlantic slave trade in the 1600s
options.D: The Hanseatic League's control of trade in the Baltic Sea

practice.explanation: In the mid-1600s Dutch ships carried goods from all over the world into Europe's ports, including England's. English leaders hoped the act would cut the Dutch out of this trade.

whyNot.A: Spain's empire was mainly in the Americas and the Philippines. In the 1600s the Dutch, not Spain, led Europe's trade with the East Indies.
whyNot.C: France's slave trade grew mainly in the 1700s. In 1651 the Portuguese and the Dutch led the trade.
whyNot.D: By the 1600s the Hanseatic League had lost most of its power, and the Dutch led trade in the Baltic.

practice.hint: Which country had Europe's largest merchant fleet in the mid-1600s?

practice.stem: The Navigation Act most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: The Thirty Years' War
options.B: The War of the Spanish Succession
options.C: The Great Northern War
options.D: The First Anglo-Dutch War

practice.explanation: The Dutch saw the act as an attack on their trade. Fights over trade and shipping led to the First Anglo-Dutch War (1652–1654). It was the first of three wars between England and the Dutch Republic in the 1600s.

whyNot.A: The Thirty Years' War ended in 1648, three years before the act.
whyNot.B: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) was fought over who would inherit Spain's throne.
whyNot.C: The Great Northern War (1700–1721) was fought mainly between Russia and Sweden.

practice.hint: Which country's merchants lost the most business because of the act?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes the point of view from which Sancho judges European traders?

options.A: He judges them as protectors who saved Africans from their own rulers.
options.B: He judges them as people whose overseas trade should be ended.
options.C: He judges them by religious ideals that their own conduct violates.
options.D: He judges them mainly by the wealth their trade adds to Britain.

practice.explanation: Sancho says God meant trade "to unite mankind" in "brotherly love." Then he shows "Christian" traders spreading greed, cruelty, and the slave trade. He judges them by the faith they claim to follow.

whyNot.A: Sancho does not praise European rule. He blames European greed for encouraging the "petty Kings" to kill and kidnap.
whyNot.B: Sancho says commerce was meant "to unite mankind," so he does not ask for trade to end. He attacks the greed and cruelty of the traders.
whyNot.D: Sancho mocks the traders' love of "money—money—money." He judges them by how they treat people, not by the wealth they bring Britain.

practice.hint: Compare what Sancho says trade was meant to do with what he says Christian traders actually do.

practice.stem: Sancho's criticism of "the Christians' abominable traffic for slaves" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The growth of the Atlantic slave trade to supply plantations
options.B: The end of the slave trade after the Peace of Utrecht in 1713
options.C: The Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca empires
options.D: Britain's abolition of slavery in its colonies

practice.explanation: In the 1600s and 1700s, Europeans wanted more sugar, tobacco, coffee, and cotton. Plantation owners in the Americas bought millions of enslaved Africans to grow these crops. Sancho condemned the trade that supplied them.

whyNot.B: The Peace of Utrecht gave Britain the right to sell enslaved Africans in Spanish America, which expanded the trade.
whyNot.C: The Spanish conquered the Aztec and Inca empires in the 1500s. Sancho writes in 1778 about the trade in enslaved Africans.
whyNot.D: Parliament passed the act ending slavery in most British colonies in 1833, and it took effect in 1834, more than fifty years after this letter.

practice.hint: Where were most enslaved Africans taken in the 1700s, and what did they produce?

practice.stem: Arguments like Sancho's most directly contributed to which later development?

options.A: The end of Britain's slave trade
options.B: The Glorious Revolution in England
options.C: The repeal of the Navigation Acts
options.D: The cut in Britain's tax on tea in 1784

practice.explanation: Writings by Black authors in Britain, such as Sancho, Olaudah Equiano, and Ottobah Cugoano, helped the fight against slavery. Parliament banned the British slave trade in 1807.

whyNot.B: The Glorious Revolution took place in 1688–1689, long before Sancho wrote in 1778.
whyNot.C: Britain repealed the Navigation Acts in 1849 because of arguments for free trade, not protests against the slave trade.
whyNot.D: Parliament cut the tea tax in 1784 to stop smuggling. Sancho's letter attacks the greed and cruelty of European traders, not taxes.

practice.hint: Sancho calls the slave trade "abominable." Which later change dealt with the problem he describes?

practice.stem: Given its context, the painting was most likely intended to

options.A: decorate a Catholic church with a scene from the life of a saint
options.B: celebrate the military victories of the Dutch prince of Orange
options.C: honor the guild officials and show that they could be trusted
options.D: warn viewers that wealth and fine clothes lead people into sin

practice.explanation: The guild ordered this group portrait for its hall in Amsterdam. It shows the officials as calm, serious men at work. This told the cloth makers and merchants who came there that the officials judged fairly.

whyNot.A: The painting shows six men at a meeting, not a saint, and it was made for the guild's hall. Dutch Reformed churches did not display religious paintings.
whyNot.B: No prince, soldier, or battle appears. The men are cloth officials at a meeting.
whyNot.D: The men are shown with respect, in plain, serious clothes. Nothing in the painting mocks them or their wealth.

practice.hint: Where did the painting hang, and who would have seen it there?

practice.stem: In the Dutch Republic in the 1600s, which group most often paid for paintings like this one?

options.A: Catholic bishops and monasteries
options.B: Merchants, guilds, and town officials
options.C: Kings, princes, and their royal households
options.D: Peasant villages and their lords

practice.explanation: The Dutch Republic was rich and run mostly by town merchants. Merchants bought paintings for their homes. Guilds and other town groups ordered group portraits like this one for their halls.

whyNot.A: The Dutch Republic was mostly Protestant, and the Catholic Church could not worship openly or order art for public churches there.
whyNot.C: The Dutch Republic had no king. Its leaders were wealthy townspeople.
whyNot.D: Most Dutch paintings were bought by people in towns, not by villages or noble lords.

practice.hint: Who held wealth and power in Dutch towns?

practice.stem: The officials shown in the painting best illustrate which feature of the early modern European economy?

options.A: Joint-stock companies that sold shares to investors
options.B: Royal ministers who ran state-owned workshops
options.C: Central banks that lent money to governments at war
options.D: Guilds that set and enforced standards for goods

practice.explanation: Guilds controlled many trades in European towns. Each year, Amsterdam's mayors and aldermen chose syndics to check the quality of cloth for the drapers' guild. Such rules protected buyers, but they could also limit competition.

whyNot.A: Joint-stock companies, such as the Dutch East India Company, raised money by selling shares. These men are guild officials who inspect cloth.
whyNot.B: The Dutch Republic had no king or royal ministers. State-run workshops were more common in France under Colbert.
whyNot.C: The men work for a cloth guild, not a bank.

practice.hint: What job did these men do for their guild?

practice.stem: The victory Sobieski describes most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople
options.B: The Holy League's naval victory at Lepanto
options.C: The Habsburg conquest of Hungary
options.D: The first partition of Poland

practice.explanation: After their defeat at Vienna in 1683, the Ottomans were pushed back. In the Treaty of Karlowitz (1699), they gave most of Hungary to the Habsburgs. Their push into central Europe was over.

whyNot.A: The Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453, more than two centuries earlier.
whyNot.B: Lepanto was a sea battle in 1571, more than a century before Vienna.
whyNot.D: The first partition of Poland came in 1772 and grew out of Poland's weakness and its neighbors' rivalry, not out of the victory at Vienna.

practice.hint: Once the Ottoman army was driven back from Vienna, which power could push east into lands the Ottomans held?

practice.stem: Sobieski most likely describes the praise he received from princes and from the people of Vienna because

options.A: he was writing privately to his wife and wanted to share his personal glory
options.B: he hoped to persuade the princes to elect him Holy Roman Emperor
options.C: he wanted to frighten the Ottoman sultan into giving up Hungary
options.D: he was answering charges that his army had arrived too late to help

practice.explanation: This is a personal letter to his wife. Sobieski tells her about the treasure, the grand vizier's escape, and the crowds "calling me their savior." He wants her to share in his glory and Poland's.

whyNot.B: This is a private letter to his wife, not a message to the German princes, and Sobieski asks for no title.
whyNot.C: The letter was written to his wife, not to the sultan.
whyNot.D: Sobieski says the town "could not have held out five days longer," so he arrived in time. He does not mention any charge against him.

practice.hint: To whom was the letter written? How might that shape what Sobieski chose to tell?

practice.stem: The alliance that fought at Vienna is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Wars of religion between Catholic and Protestant princes in Germany
options.B: France's alliance with the Habsburgs against the Ottoman sultan
options.C: Poland's war to win its independence from the Holy Roman Empire
options.D: Habsburg-Ottoman rivalry for control of central Europe

practice.explanation: Since the 1500s the Ottomans and the Austrian Habsburgs had fought over Hungary and the lands along the Danube River. In 1683 the Ottomans attacked Vienna. The emperor's allies, including Poland and German princes, came to save it.

whyNot.A: Germany's religious wars ended in 1648. At Vienna, princes of the Holy Roman Empire fought together against the Ottomans.
whyNot.B: France was the Habsburgs' main rival and did not join the fight at Vienna.
whyNot.C: Poland was not part of the Holy Roman Empire. Sobieski came as the emperor's ally.

practice.hint: Which two powers had been fighting over Hungary and the Danube lands since the 1500s?

practice.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 refuses Charles II's will, while Source 2 urges the Duke of Anjou to accept it.
options.B: Source 1 is mainly concerned with trade, while Source 2 is mainly concerned with religion.
options.C: Source 1 links the inheritance to peace, while Source 2 calls it a danger to Europe.
options.D: Source 1 claims Spain's lands for the emperor, while Source 2 claims them for France.

practice.explanation: Louis XIV says Charles II wanted "the general quiet of all Europe" and promises to keep the peace. The allies say France and Spain together could "assume to themselves the dominion over all Europe."

whyNot.A: Source 1 says "We accept" the will for Louis's grandson. Source 2 objects to the will.
whyNot.B: Source 2, not Source 1, worries about "Navigation and Commerce." Neither source is mainly about religion.
whyNot.D: Source 1 accepts the lands for Louis XIV's grandson, the Duke of Anjou. Source 2 supports the emperor's claim.

practice.hint: How does each source describe what the inheritance will mean for the rest of Europe?

practice.stem: The concerns expressed in Source 2 most directly reflect which goal of European diplomacy after 1648?

options.A: Restoring the religious unity of Christian Europe under the pope
options.B: Keeping any one state from growing strong enough to dominate the rest
options.C: Protecting the rights of subjects against the power of their kings
options.D: Spreading republican government to the monarchies of Europe

practice.explanation: The allies feared that France and Spain together would "become so formidable to all" that they could rule Europe. Keeping one power from ruling the rest is called the balance of power.

whyNot.A: After 1648, religion mattered less in wars between European states. The allies included both Catholic and Protestant rulers.
whyNot.C: The treaty is about the claims and safety of rulers and states. It says nothing about subjects' rights.
whyNot.D: The emperor and William III were monarchs, and the alliance did not try to turn monarchies into republics.

practice.hint: What do the allies fear will happen if France and Spain become "one and the same kingdom"?

practice.stem: The war that followed the events in the sources most directly resulted in which of the following?

options.A: Louis XIV's grandson kept Spain's throne but gave up his claim to France's.
options.B: The emperor's son became king of Spain and ruled its empire in the Americas.
options.C: France took over the Spanish Netherlands as a barrier against the Dutch.
options.D: Spain's colonies in the Americas were divided between Britain and the Dutch.

practice.explanation: The War of the Spanish Succession (1701–1714) ended with the treaties of Utrecht (1713) and of Rastatt and Baden (1714). Louis XIV's grandson stayed king of Spain as Philip V. But he gave up his claim to France, so the two crowns stayed apart.

whyNot.B: The emperor's son Charles fought for the Spanish throne but did not win it. In 1711 he became Holy Roman Emperor instead.
whyNot.C: The Spanish Netherlands went to Austria, not France, in the peace treaties of 1713–1714.
whyNot.D: Spain kept its colonies in the Americas. Britain gained trading rights there, such as the right to sell enslaved Africans.

practice.hint: The allies feared France and Spain becoming "one and the same kingdom." What compromise could prevent that?

practice.stem: The edict most directly resulted in which of the following?

options.A: The flight of many Huguenots abroad
options.B: The outbreak of the French Wars of Religion
options.C: The revolts of the Fronde against the crown
options.D: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy

practice.explanation: Article X said Huguenots could not leave. Even so, perhaps 150,000 or more fled after 1685. Many went to the Dutch Republic, England, and Brandenburg-Prussia, where they used their skills in trade and crafts.

whyNot.B: The French Wars of Religion began in 1562 and ended with the Edict of Nantes in 1598.
whyNot.C: The Fronde revolts took place from 1648 to 1653, decades before 1685.
whyNot.D: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy was passed during the French Revolution, in 1790.

practice.hint: Article X forbids Protestants to leave France. Why would the king need such a rule?

practice.stem: The edict best illustrates which goal of Louis XIV's government?

options.A: Making the French Catholic Church independent of royal control
options.B: Extending royal control over the religious life of French subjects
options.C: Winning support from Protestant powers such as England
options.D: Raising money by selling Protestant church buildings

practice.explanation: Louis XIV wanted his kingdom to share one faith as well as one king. By ending the Edict of Nantes, he used royal power to force religious unity. He controlled France's government and army in the same way.

whyNot.A: The edict is the king's own decision about how his subjects may worship. It does not free the Church from royal control.
whyNot.C: The edict angered Protestant states, and many Huguenots fled to them.
whyNot.D: The edict forbids Protestant worship. It does not mention selling church buildings.

practice.hint: Who decides here how French people may worship?

practice.stem: Which of the following most limits the edict's usefulness as evidence of how many French Protestants had truly accepted the Catholic faith?

options.A: Protestants in France still outnumbered Catholics in the 1680s.
options.B: Many conversions had been forced by soldiers lodged in Protestant homes.
options.C: The king had no reliable way to learn what religion his subjects followed.
options.D: Most Huguenots had left France well before 1685.

practice.explanation: In the early 1680s royal officials sent soldiers, called dragoons, to live in Protestant homes until the families converted. Many conversions were forced in this way. So a recorded conversion does not prove that a person truly accepted Catholic beliefs.

whyNot.A: Catholics were a large majority in France. Protestants were a small minority.
whyNot.C: Royal officials sent the king reports on conversions. The problem is how the conversions were won, not whether they could be counted.
whyNot.D: Article X shows that many Protestants were still in France and had to be forbidden to leave. Most of the flight came after 1685.

practice.hint: How might the king's officials have won so many conversions so quickly?

practice.stem: Burnet's account would be most useful to a historian studying

options.A: how Peter's interests and character struck an Anglican bishop
options.B: how ordinary Russians felt about Peter's plans to change their customs
options.C: how Peter's later wars against Sweden were planned and fought
