options.D: how the Russian Church reacted to Peter's control of its leaders

practice.explanation: Burnet spent many hours with Peter in England. His account shows how an Anglican bishop saw the young tsar: clever and hardworking, but hot-tempered. It tells us much less about Russia itself.

whyNot.B: Burnet describes his own talks with Peter in England. The excerpt gives no views from ordinary Russians.
whyNot.C: Burnet describes Peter's visit in 1698, two years before Russia's war with Sweden began in 1700.
whyNot.D: Burnet says Peter "did not seem disposed to mend matters in Moscovy," but he gives no Russian church leader's views.

practice.hint: Where did Burnet meet Peter, and with whom did he talk?

practice.stem: Peter's plan "to polish his people" most directly led to which of the following later policies?

options.A: Freedom for Russia's serfs
options.B: Western dress and schooling for nobles
options.C: Restoration of the patriarch's power
options.D: An elected assembly to advise the tsar

practice.explanation: Back from Europe, Peter made nobles at court shave their beards and wear Western clothes. He sent young nobles abroad to study and opened schools for math and sailing. Catherine the Great later continued these changes.

whyNot.A: Peter made serfdom heavier to support his army and state. Russia's serfs were not freed until 1861.
whyNot.C: Peter left the office of patriarch empty and in 1721 replaced it with a church council, the Holy Synod, under state control.
whyNot.D: Peter ruled as an absolute monarch and did not create an elected assembly.

practice.hint: Burnet says Peter planned to send Russians "to travel in other countries." What would he want them to bring home?

practice.stem: Peter's plan for "a great fleet at Azuph" to attack the Turkish empire is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Russia's wars to win ports on the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea
options.B: Russia's alliance with the Ottoman Empire against Sweden
options.C: Russia's plans to found colonies across the Atlantic in the Americas
options.D: Russia's efforts to spread Orthodox Christianity to western Europe

practice.explanation: Russia had few seaports that did not freeze. Peter fought the Ottomans for Azov, near the Black Sea. Then he fought Sweden from 1700 to 1721 to win land on the Baltic Sea, where he built St. Petersburg.

whyNot.B: Russia and the Ottomans were enemies. Peter captured Azov from the Ottomans in 1696.
whyNot.C: Russia later expanded across the Pacific into Alaska, but in 1698 Peter's goal was seaports close to Europe.
whyNot.D: Peter wanted to learn from western Europe, not convert it. Burnet says Peter planned "to draw strangers to come and live among" Russians.

practice.hint: Look at a map: where could Russian ships reach the open sea?

exam.title: Unit 3 Practice Exam: Absolutism and Constitutionalism
exam.directions: Each set of questions refers to a source: a primary source, a historian's writing, an image, or data. For each question, choose the best answer. Use the source and your knowledge of European history from c. 1648 to c. 1815. There is no penalty for guessing. Some sources use historical labels or words for groups of people that are no longer used; these words show the language of their time.

questions.stem: The measures described in the letter are most clearly an example of which economic policy?

options.A: Laissez-faire
options.B: Physiocracy
options.C: Manorialism
options.D: Mercantilism

rationales.A: Incorrect. Laissez-faire means the government leaves the economy alone. Here the king spends royal money to direct trade and industry.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Physiocrats were French thinkers of the 1750s and 1760s who said land and farming were the source of wealth and called for free trade. This letter is from 1664 and is about trade and manufactures.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Manorialism was the medieval system in which peasants worked a lord's land. The letter is about trade, shipping, and workshops.
rationales.D: Correct. The king sets aside royal money for workshops and shipping and supports trading companies so that France can make and sell more and depend less on other countries.

questions.explanation: Mercantilism tried to make the state rich and strong through trade, industry, shipping, and colonies. The government often helped. Here Louis XIV pays money to workshops and shippers and supports trading companies.

questions.stem: The letter best illustrates which development in France under Louis XIV?

options.A: Provincial nobles took charge of the kingdom's economic policy.
options.B: Merchants won the right to elect members of the king's councils.
options.C: The king's government directed the growth of trade and industry.
options.D: The Catholic Church took over the regulation of trade and prices.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The letter goes from the king to the town and points merchants to a royal minister, Colbert. It does not give provincial nobles control of economic policy.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The king tells merchants to bring their concerns to Sieur Colbert. They do not elect anyone to his councils.
rationales.C: Correct. The king creates a council of commerce to meet "in our presence," pays help from the "royal treasury," and tells merchants to deal with his minister, Colbert.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The letter says nothing about the Church. Trade is directed by the king and his minister.

questions.explanation: Louis XIV and his minister Colbert used royal councils, money from the treasury, and trading companies to promote French trade and industry. The letter places these policies under the king's direction.

questions.stem: The plan to abolish tolls on France's rivers is best seen as part of which broader change in the European economy?

options.A: Guilds' growing power to set the prices of goods across whole kingdoms
options.B: States' decisions to stop taxing goods brought in from other countries
options.C: A return to trade by barter as gold and silver became scarce in Europe
options.D: States' efforts to remove local barriers to trade inside their own borders

rationales.A: Incorrect. Guilds controlled trades in individual towns. Freeing trade from local controls worked against their power.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Mercantilist states such as France raised taxes on foreign goods to protect their own industries. Colbert raised these tariffs in 1667.
rationales.C: Incorrect. In the 1600s European trade relied more and more on money, credit, and banks, as American silver flowed into Europe.
rationales.D: Correct. Local tolls raised the cost of moving goods inside a country. Rulers who wanted one national economy tried to remove them.

questions.explanation: Towns, lords, and provinces collected tolls on rivers and roads. By removing these tolls, France tried to let goods move freely inside the kingdom. This was part of a long move away from local limits on trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 says the king ruled in trust for the people, while Source 2 says no earthly court may judge a king.
options.B: Source 1 calls for restoring the king with new limits, while Source 2 calls for creating a republic.
options.C: Source 1 blames the war on the king's advisers, while Source 2 blames it on foreign invaders.
options.D: Source 1 says the king was chosen by Parliament, while Source 2 says kings are chosen by the people.

rationales.A: Correct. Source 1 says Charles was "trusted with a limited power to govern by and according to the laws." Source 2 says "no earthly power can justly call me (who am your King) in question."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Source 1 charges the king with treason; it does not seek to restore him. Source 2 is the king's own defense, not a call for a republic.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Source 1 blames "the said Charles Stuart" himself for the wars. Source 2 does not discuss the causes of the war.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Source 1 says Charles was "admitted King," not chosen by Parliament. Source 2 says obedience to kings is commanded by God.

questions.explanation: The charge says the king was trusted with power "for the good and benefit of the people" and broke that trust. Charles answers that kings answer to God. He says no court, least of all this "pretended Court," can try him.

questions.stem: The trial described in the sources most directly resulted in which of the following?

options.A: The execution of the king
options.B: The Restoration of the Stuarts
options.C: The Glorious Revolution
options.D: The union of England and Scotland

rationales.A: Correct. The court found Charles guilty, and he was beheaded on January 30, 1649. The monarchy and the House of Lords were abolished soon after.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Charles II returned to the throne in 1660, eleven years later, after the Commonwealth fell apart.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Glorious Revolution came in 1688–1689, when James II was replaced by William and Mary.
rationales.D: Incorrect. England and Scotland were joined into one kingdom by the Act of Union in 1707.

questions.explanation: The court found Charles I guilty of treason, and he was executed in January 1649. His death shocked Europe's rulers. England then became a republic, the Commonwealth, until 1660.

questions.stem: Charles's argument in Source 2 most closely reflects which political idea?

options.A: Popular sovereignty
options.B: Parliamentary supremacy
options.C: Divine-right monarchy
options.D: Freedom of religious worship

rationales.A: Incorrect. Popular sovereignty means that power comes from the people. That is closer to Source 1's claim that the king was "trusted" with power for the people's benefit.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Charles denies that the House of Commons can "erect a Court of Judicature" to try him. He rejects Parliament's supremacy.
rationales.C: Correct. Charles says "the authority of obedience unto Kings" is "commanded" in the Bible and that "the King can do no wrong."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Charles does not discuss freedom of worship. He argues about who has the right to judge a king.

questions.explanation: Charles says kings answer to God, not to any "earthly power." This is the idea of divine-right monarchy. His father, James I, had argued the same thing.

questions.stem: Given its context, the portrait was most likely intended to

options.A: show the king's humility as a servant of the people of France
options.B: display the king's majesty and power to visitors at court
options.C: record the king's victory in a battle against the Dutch Republic
options.D: mock the king's vanity on behalf of his critics among the nobles

rationales.A: Incorrect. The king's rich robe, crown, and grand pose show glory and power, not humility.
rationales.B: Correct. The coronation robe, crown, scepter, sword, and grand setting all present Louis XIV as a powerful and majestic ruler.
rationales.C: Incorrect. No battle or enemy appears. The king stands in a palace room surrounded by symbols of royal power.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Rigaud was a court painter, and the portrait treats the king with great respect. It does not mock him.

questions.explanation: Louis XIV used art, buildings, and ceremony to show that he was the center of the state. This portrait shows him in his coronation robes with symbols of royal power.

questions.stem: Which earlier development most directly shaped Louis XIV's efforts to strengthen and display royal power, as seen in the portrait?

options.A: The Fronde
options.B: The Edict of Nantes
options.C: The Peace of Westphalia
options.D: The Glorious Revolution

rationales.A: Correct. During the Fronde (1648–1653), nobles and the Parlement of Paris rose against the crown while Louis was a boy. He grew up determined to keep the nobles under control.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Edict of Nantes (1598) gave French Protestants rights. Louis XIV later revoked it, but the Fronde more directly explains his fear of rebellion and his effort to control the nobles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) ended the Thirty Years' War and weakened the Holy Roman Empire. It did not set off Louis's efforts to control his own nobles.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Glorious Revolution (1688–1689) limited the English monarchy. Louis XIV's way of ruling had been set long before.

questions.explanation: As a child, Louis XIV saw nobles and Paris rebel against the crown in the Fronde. As king, he ruled without a chief minister and kept great nobles busy at Versailles. He used art like this portrait to show that all power came from him.

questions.stem: The kind of kingship shown in the portrait differed most from the English monarchy after 1689 in that Louis XIV

options.A: handed command of the royal army over to an assembly of great nobles
options.B: did not need an elected assembly's consent for taxes and laws
options.C: claimed no religious basis for his right to rule
options.D: was chosen by an assembly of nobles rather than by birth

rationales.A: Incorrect. Louis XIV kept command of the army himself and made it larger and more firmly under the crown's control.
rationales.B: Correct. After 1689 English monarchs needed Parliament's consent for taxes, laws, and a peacetime army. France's Estates-General did not meet at all between 1614 and 1789.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Louis XIV claimed to rule by divine right, with the support of writers such as Bishop Bossuet.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Louis XIV inherited the throne from his father. Kings were elected by nobles in Poland, not in France.

questions.explanation: In England after 1689, Parliament had to approve taxes and laws. Louis XIV never called France's Estates-General. He made laws on his own authority, as an absolute monarch.

questions.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the data in the table?

options.A: Legal tea sales fell during most of the 1700s as smuggling grew.
options.B: Legal tea sales were highest when the tax on tea was highest.
options.C: The tax on tea stayed about the same from 1713 to 1793.
options.D: Legal tea sales jumped after the tax on tea was cut to 12.5 percent.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Sales rose from 0.3 million pounds a year in 1713–1721 to 8.1 million in 1768–1772, so they did not fall during most of the century.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The highest tax shown, 128 percent, came in 1734–1744, when sales were 1.5 million pounds a year. The highest sales came when the tax was lowest.
rationales.C: Incorrect. In the table, the tax ranges from 12.5 percent to 128 percent of the sale price, so it did not stay about the same.
rationales.D: Correct. Sales were 5.9 million pounds in 1783, when the tax was 114 percent. With the tax at 12.5 percent, sales were 15.1 million pounds in 1785 and 16.7 million a year in 1786–1793.

questions.explanation: Legal tea sales grew during the century. Then they jumped when the tax fell to 12.5 percent. In 1784 Parliament cut the tax so much that legal tea could compete with smuggled tea.

questions.stem: The overall rise in tea sales from 1713 to 1772 is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: Britain's growing supply of tea from its own colonies in India
options.B: Britain's laws against printed cotton cloth from India
options.C: The growth of European demand for goods made in Britain
options.D: A consumer culture that made overseas goods part of daily life

rationales.A: Incorrect. In these years the Company bought its tea in China. Tea plantations in British India began only in the 1830s.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Calico Acts of 1700 and 1721 limited cotton cloth from India to protect British wool and silk makers. They did not cause the rise in tea sales.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The table records tea sold at the Company's London auctions. It does not show British goods sold to other Europeans.
rationales.D: Correct. In the 1700s tea, sugar, coffee, and tobacco from Asia and the Americas became everyday goods for many Europeans, not just for the rich.

questions.explanation: As trade with Asia and the Americas grew, tea and sugar became cheaper and more common in Britain. Many families began to drink sweet tea every day. This was part of a new consumer culture.

questions.stem: Temple's description of the Dutch government best supports which of the following conclusions?

options.A: The Dutch Republic was governed by merchant elites who ran it to promote trade.
options.B: The Dutch Republic was ruled by an absolute monarch who controlled its trade.
options.C: The Dutch Republic was governed by landed nobles who kept merchants out of power.
options.D: The Dutch Republic was governed by officials chosen by the votes of ordinary townsmen.

rationales.A: Correct. Temple says the government was "managed either by men that trade, or whose families have risen by it," which made sure trade got "all favour."
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Dutch Republic had no king. Temple describes a government run by merchants and townsmen.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Temple says the men who governed were traders or men "born and bred in towns."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Dutch town governments were run by small groups of wealthy families who chose their own members. Ordinary men did not vote for them.

questions.explanation: The Dutch Republic was ruled by a small group of rich town families and landowners. Many of them made their money in trade. So they used the government to protect and grow trade.

questions.stem: Temple's praise for "the use of their banks" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Catholic Church's ban on lending at interest, which the Dutch enforced strictly
options.B: Dutch merchants' use of gold from mines in Dutch colonies
options.C: The collapse of British credit after the South Sea Bubble of 1720
options.D: New financial institutions, such as the Bank of Amsterdam, that eased payments

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Dutch Republic was mostly Protestant, and Dutch lenders charged interest openly. Cheap credit helped Dutch trade.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Dutch did not own large gold mines in their colonies. Their wealth came from trade and shipping.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The South Sea Bubble burst in 1720, almost fifty years after Temple wrote.
rationales.D: Correct. The Bank of Amsterdam, founded in 1609, held merchants' money and let them pay one another safely, making trade "quick," as Temple says.

questions.explanation: In the 1600s Amsterdam had Europe's leading bank and stock exchange. These new institutions made it easier for merchants to pay, borrow, and invest. This helped the Dutch lead European trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how the Dutch position Temple describes changed during the 1700s?

options.A: The Dutch Republic conquered the Spanish Netherlands and became a great land power.
options.B: Britain overtook the Dutch Republic as Europe's leading trading and naval power.
options.C: The Dutch Republic became an absolute monarchy under the princes of Orange.
options.D: The Dutch Republic took over France's colonies in North America.

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Spanish Netherlands passed to Austria in 1713–1714, not to the Dutch Republic.
rationales.B: Correct. After costly wars against Louis XIV, the Dutch Republic declined as a great power, while Britain's navy, trade, and empire grew.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The princes of Orange served as stadtholders, but the Dutch Republic did not become an absolute monarchy in the 1700s.
rationales.D: Incorrect. France lost Canada and other North American lands to Britain in 1763, not to the Dutch.

questions.explanation: Long wars against France wore down the Dutch Republic. Meanwhile Britain built a bigger navy and empire. By the late 1700s London had replaced Amsterdam as the center of world trade.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Queen Anne's main argument in the speech?

options.A: Britain should keep fighting until France gives up its colonies in North America.
options.B: The peace would keep France and Spain apart and win trade advantages for Britain.
options.C: The peace would place the emperor's son on the throne of Spain.
options.D: Parliament alone should decide whether Britain makes war or makes peace.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Anne is announcing terms of peace, not calling for more war. Under these terms France kept Quebec and the rest of Canada, which it did not lose until 1763.
rationales.B: Correct. Anne says France and Spain will be "more effectually divided than ever" and lists gains such as Gibraltar, Minorca, Newfoundland, and the Asiento.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Anne accepts the Duke of Anjou as king of Spain, as long as he gives up all claim to the crown of France. The emperor's son did not get Spain.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Anne says making peace and war is "the undoubted Prerogative of the Crown." She informs Parliament but does not hand it the decision.

questions.explanation: Anne says the peace keeps France and Spain apart, which was "the chief Inducement to begin this War." She says it creates "a real Balance of Power." She also lists new lands and trading rights for Britain.

questions.stem: The agreement described in the last paragraph most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: End of slavery in Spanish America
options.B: Decline of Caribbean sugar production
options.C: Growth of Britain's slave trade
options.D: French control of Britain's trade with Spain

rationales.A: Incorrect. Slavery continued in Spanish America into the 1800s. The Asiento brought more enslaved people there.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Sugar production in the Caribbean grew in the 1700s, and planters bought more enslaved Africans to work the fields.
rationales.C: Correct. The Asiento let British merchants, through the South Sea Company, sell enslaved Africans in Spanish America. Britain became the leading slave-trading nation of the 1700s.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Asiento passed from France to Britain. Anne says it had been "enjoyed by the French for these Ten Years past."

questions.explanation: The Asiento let Britain sell enslaved Africans in Spain's American colonies for thirty years. Along with Britain's own sugar colonies, it helped make Britain the leading slave-trading country of the 1700s.

questions.stem: Anne's concern for "the Protestant Succession … in the House of Hanover" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: The Peace of Westphalia's rule that each prince could choose his state's religion
options.B: The Edict of Nantes, which protected the rights of Protestants in France
options.C: Henry VIII's break with Rome over the end of his first marriage
options.D: Laws after the Glorious Revolution that kept Catholics from the throne

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Peace of Westphalia dealt with the princes of the Holy Roman Empire. It did not decide who would rule Britain.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Edict of Nantes protected French Protestants, and Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. It did not apply to Britain.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Henry VIII broke with Rome in the 1530s. The question of a Catholic heir arose again after James II became a Catholic.
rationales.D: Correct. The Bill of Rights (1689) barred Catholics from the throne, and the Act of Settlement (1701) named Sophia of Hanover and her Protestant heirs as next in line.

questions.explanation: After Catholic James II lost the throne in 1688, the Bill of Rights barred Catholics from the throne. Anne's last living child died in 1700. So in 1701 the Act of Settlement named Sophia of Hanover, a Protestant granddaughter of James I, and her Protestant heirs to rule after William III and Anne. This shut out James II's Catholic son.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the two sources?

options.A: Source 1 blames Prussia for the partition, while Source 2 blames Russia for it.
options.B: Source 1 calls the partition a lawful way to restore order, while Source 2 calls it shameful.
options.C: Source 1 says Poland's king asked for the partition, while Source 2 says Poland's nobles asked for it.
options.D: Source 1 rejects the partition, while Source 2 supports it as good for Austria.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Source 1 says the three powers acted together. Source 2 blames hard times and Austria's isolation, not Russia alone.
rationales.B: Correct. Source 1 speaks of the powers' "rights and claims" and of a plan "to restore peace and good order in Poland." Maria Theresa calls the partition "a blot on my whole reign."
rationales.C: Incorrect. Source 1 says the three powers came to an agreement among themselves. Neither source says that the Polish king or nobles asked for a partition.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Source 1 announces the partition. Maria Theresa says she agreed to it only after refusing "many times."

questions.explanation: The declaration says the partition restores order and sets safe borders. In a private letter, Maria Theresa admits she agreed only under pressure. She calls it "a blot on my whole reign."

questions.stem: The "disorders" in Poland described in Source 1 are best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.A: A Protestant revolt against Poland's Catholic kings and bishops
options.B: Pugachev's peasant revolt against serfdom
options.C: Polish nobles' power to elect kings and block laws in their parliament
options.D: Poland's war with Sweden for the Baltic coast

rationales.A: Incorrect. The nobles who rose in arms in 1768 were mainly Catholics who opposed Russia's demands for more rights for Protestant and Orthodox Christians.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Pugachev's revolt broke out in Russia in 1773, not in Poland. The fighting in Poland was among nobles and their followers.
rationales.C: Correct. Polish nobles elected their kings, and a single deputy could break up the diet with the liberum veto. Rival noble groups invited foreign powers to take sides.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Poland's great wars with Sweden came in the 1600s and early 1700s. In 1772 Russia was at war with the Ottoman Empire.

questions.explanation: Poland's elected kings had little power over the nobles. In the 1760s Polish nobles formed armed groups against the king and against Russia. Poland's neighbors used this disorder as an excuse to take its land.

questions.stem: The three powers' agreement to divide Polish lands among themselves best reflects which principle?

options.A: Popular sovereignty
options.B: Divine-right monarchy
options.C: The balance of power
options.D: Religious toleration

rationales.A: Incorrect. The Polish people were not asked. The three rulers made the decision after "having come to an agreement" among themselves.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Divine right is about where a king's power comes from. This agreement is about relations among rival states.
rationales.C: Correct. Each power gained land, so none of the three gained too much compared with the others. Their shares were not equal, but the deal kept a balance among them.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The agreement says nothing about religion. It is about dividing land.

questions.explanation: Russia, Prussia, and Austria each took Polish land. The shares were not equal, but each power gained something, so none of them gained too much compared with the others. This helped them avoid a war with one another.

questions.stem: In the long term, the events described in the sources contributed most directly to which of the following?

options.A: The disappearance of the Polish state
options.B: A stronger Polish monarchy backed by its neighbors
options.C: A Prussian alliance that protected Poland from Russia
options.D: Polish control of trade on the Baltic Sea

rationales.A: Correct. In the Second Partition (1793), Russia and Prussia took more Polish land. In the Third (1795), Russia, Prussia, and Austria divided the rest. Poland did not exist again as an independent state until 1918.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Polish reformers tried to strengthen the government with a new constitution in 1791, but Russia sent troops against it in 1792.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Prussia signed an alliance with Poland in 1790 but did not defend Poland when Russia attacked in 1792. In 1793 Prussia joined Russia in taking more Polish land.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The first partition gave Prussia most of Poland's Baltic coast. Prussia took the port of Danzig in 1793.

questions.explanation: The first partition took almost a third of Poland's land. Polish reformers tried to make the state stronger. But Russia and Prussia took more land in 1793, and in 1795 the three powers divided the rest.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Waliszewski's main argument?

options.A: Peter invented a new program of reform that no earlier tsar had imagined or attempted.
options.B: Peter's reforms were slow and peaceful because he consulted his nobles before acting.
options.C: Peter carried on earlier tsars' plans, but war and his temper made them violent.
options.D: Peter's reforms were driven mainly by the demands of Russia's merchants and towns.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Waliszewski asks what new thing Peter did and answers, "Nothing, or, at most, very little indeed."
rationales.B: Incorrect. Waliszewski says Peter's measures were marked by "violence, excess and hastiness."
rationales.C: Correct. Waliszewski says of the earlier tsars' plan, "The programme above referred to was his programme." He says war and Peter's "violence, excess and hastiness" turned "a peaceful evolution" into "a revolution."
rationales.D: Incorrect. Waliszewski names war, Peter's own tastes, and his temper as the forces behind the reforms. He does not mention merchants' demands.

questions.explanation: Waliszewski says earlier tsars had already planned to rebuild the army, the money system, and trade. Peter's long wars and fierce temper made those plans move fast and with force.

questions.stem: Which of the following, if true, would best support Waliszewski's claim that "the war made military reforms a first necessity, and these called forth financial measures"?

options.A: Peter created a new tax on each male peasant to pay for his growing army.
options.B: Peter ordered nobles at court to shave their beards and wear Western clothes.
options.C: Peter replaced the head of the Russian Church with a council under state control.
options.D: Peter founded an Academy of Sciences to bring Western learning to Russia.

rationales.A: Correct. A tax created to pay for the army shows a military need leading to a financial measure, just as the claim says. Peter's poll tax of the 1720s did this.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Rules about beards and dress reflect what Waliszewski calls Peter's "tastes" and "fancies," not the needs of war.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Replacing the patriarch with the Holy Synod increased Peter's control of the Church. It was not mainly a way to pay for war.
rationales.D: Incorrect. The Academy of Sciences, which Peter planned and which opened in 1725, aimed at learning. It does not show war leading to financial measures.

questions.explanation: Waliszewski says war came first. A bigger army needed money, and that led to new taxes. Peter's tax on male peasants, collected from the 1720s, was created to pay for his army.

questions.stem: Peter's efforts to strengthen his army and central government while keeping supreme authority in his own hands were most similar to the efforts of which of the following leaders?

options.A: William III of England
options.B: Louis XIV of France
options.C: Stanisław II Augustus of Poland
options.D: Johan de Witt of the Dutch Republic

rationales.A: Incorrect. William III also built up England's army, but he ruled within the limits of the Bill of Rights. He needed Parliament's consent for taxes and a peacetime army.
rationales.B: Correct. Like Peter, Louis XIV built a large standing army, expanded the central government, and brought the church and the nobles under royal control, while keeping final power in his own hands.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stanisław II was an elected king who could not control Poland's nobles, and his country was partitioned.
rationales.D: Incorrect. De Witt led the Dutch Republic, a merchant republic without a king, from 1653 to 1672.

questions.explanation: Peter and Louis XIV were both absolute monarchs. Both built large armies, raised heavy taxes, and grew the central government. Both made nobles serve the crown, and neither shared supreme power with an elected assembly.

questions.stem: In the long term, the changes Waliszewski describes most directly contributed to which of the following?

options.A: Russia's rise as a great power that took land from its neighbors
options.B: Russia's adoption of a constitution limiting the tsar
options.C: The end of serfdom in Russia under Catherine the Great
options.D: Russia's return to the old customs that Peter had banned

rationales.A: Correct. Peter defeated Sweden in the Great Northern War, and under Catherine the Great Russia won land from the Ottomans and took part in the partitions of Poland.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Russia had no constitution limiting the tsar until the early 1900s.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Serfdom grew harsher under Catherine the Great. It was not ended until 1861.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Later rulers, especially Catherine the Great, continued Peter's westernizing policies rather than undoing them.

questions.explanation: Peter's new army and navy beat Sweden in 1721, and Russia gained land on the Baltic Sea. Later, Catherine the Great won land on the Black Sea and much of Poland. Russia became one of Europe's great powers.
